paras: The exclusion of Black people from Forsyth County, Georgia, was reported in late August 1915, when an Atlanta dispatch stated that all Black people had been barred from entering the county after trouble between whites and blacks there and in neighboring territory. The dispatch illustrated the ban with an incident at Cumming, where a crowd of several hundred threatened two Black servants of an Atlanta visitor with violence unless they left the county at once. The story ran in white papers from Virginia to Missouri and was reprinted in Black weeklies into mid-September.

According to the Richmond Virginian's version of the dispatch, several reports of trouble had reached Atlanta, trouble that "dates back to the murder of a white girl and the lynching of a couple of negroes and the legal hanging of another," while troops guarded against "mob interference." That version gave no names, dates or places for the girl's death, the lynchings or the hanging, and the other versions omitted the passage entirely.

Hudson Moore, described as "a prominent Atlantan" and in another version as "a prominent white man," went to Cumming (printed "Cummings") on legal business, taking a Black nurse and a Black chauffeur with him. While he was in the courthouse he heard a commotion outside and found a crowd of several hundred gathered around the two, threatening them with violence if they did not leave the county at once. Moore intervened, talked to the crowd, pushed the two into his automobile and drove them some fifteen miles out of the county, where he left them and returned to finish his business.
The Butler Weekly Times version, dated Atlanta, August 28, placed the incident "yesterday," that is, on August 27. No version named the nurse or the chauffeur or reported that either was injured.

No report of arrests, an investigation or any official response to the crowd at Cumming appears in the coverage. The dispatch also did not say how the bar on Black people entering the county was enforced beyond this incident.

The earliest versions appeared on August 28 in the Richmond Virginian, under the front-page headline "BAR ALL NEGROES FROM FORSYTH COUNTY," and in the Washington Times, under "Georgia County Bars Negroes; Two Rescued." The two papers printed different parts of what appears to be the same dispatch: the Richmond Virginian kept only the background of murder, lynching, hanging and troops, while the Washington Times kept only the Moore incident. A reworded version headed "Georgia County Bars Blacks" ran in the Butler Weekly Times of Missouri on September 2, and the Clarksburg Sunday Telegram of West Virginia reprinted the Washington Times text on September 12 under "NEGROES BARRED" and the subhead "Prominent Atlanta Man Rescues Two from a Large Crowd," with the dateline moved to September 11. Beyond the headlines, which cast Moore as a rescuer, the white papers added no comment, except for a one-line item the New Britain Herald of Connecticut took from the Rochester Union: "Forsyth County, Georgia, refuses to allow negroes within her borders. Lucky negroes."

In the Black press, the St. Paul Appeal ran the story on September 4 as "COUNTY BARS COLORED MEN," with the subhead "Two Servants of Prominent Atlantic [Atlantan] Driven from Cummings, Ga." and an Augusta dateline, and it ran the same item again on September 18. The Appeal's text replaced "negroes" with "colored men," stating that "all colored men have been barred from entering the county." The Colorado Statesman on September 11 and the Omaha Monitor on September 18 printed the Butler Weekly Times wording under an Atlanta, September 3, dateline, capitalizing "Colored" and "Negroes." None of the Black weeklies added comment, and none carried the passage about the girl's murder and the lynchings.

The date of the Cumming incident rests on the earliest datelines, Atlanta, August 27 and 28, with the Butler Weekly Times putting it on the day before its August 28 dateline. Later printings carried datelines of September 3 and September 11, or an Augusta dateline with "today," which appear to reflect reprinting rather than separate events.

reader.title: Exclusion of Black people from Forsyth County, Georgia (1915)
bases: The dispatch reported that all Black people had been barred from entering Forsyth County and that a crowd of several hundred at Cumming threatened two Black servants with violence unless they left the county at once, after which they were driven out (A1, A2, A3).

In the reported episode a crowd of several hundred threatened two Black people with violence to make them leave the county, and no one was killed (A2, A3). The lynching of 'a couple of negroes' appears only as undated background in one version of the dispatch (A1) and is an earlier, separate event with no names, date or place.
Every article descends from one Atlanta dispatch, printed in variant editions and reprinted (A1, A2, A3, A4); no local Georgia report or independent account was found.
